name: The three-class Utopia (guardians, soldiers, producers)
plain_explanation: Plato divides his ideal city into ordinary workers, soldiers (auxiliaries), and a small ruling class of 'guardians' who alone hold political power, with movement between classes possible only in exceptional cases.
precise_definition: Plato's tripartite social structure in which political authority is restricted to a numerically small guardian class (chosen initially by the legislator, thereafter mainly hereditary, with exceptional promotion or demotion based on merit), a larger soldier class enforcing the guardians' will, and the mass of common people engaged in productive labor.
why_it_mattered: It is the structural backbone of the entire Utopia: nearly every other institution Russell discusses (education, property, family, the noble lie) exists to keep this class structure stable and to ensure the guardians govern as intended.
historical_origin: Modeled partly on Spartan social structure (citizens vs. helots vs. perioeci), discussed in the previous chapter.
examples: Russell compares the guardians to 'the Jesuits in old Paraguay, the ecclesiastics in the States of the Church until 1870, and the Communist Party in the U.S.S.R.'
influence_on_later_thinkers: The template of a specially trained, ideologically committed governing minority recurs across later utopian and revolutionary political theory.
